title: The Sealed Reckoning-Vault
subtitle: Two Hundred Years of Raw Observations, Behind a Mechanism Nobody Living Has Opened

setting.name: The Computing Rooms, the Undercroft and the Vault
setting.description: Days three and four inside the House. Upstairs: four long rooms of sloped desks, three years of published tables in bound quires, and the Master's study with a day-book that has a page cut out of it close to the gutter. Downstairs: barrel-vaulted cellars, the winter's stores, the bursar's counting-room, the cold-store with a body in it, and at the far end an iron-bound door with a mechanism of dials and cranks in its face. Behind that door are two centuries of raw nightly observations — the measurements from which every published table was computed — and the mechanism opens to a sequence that was held in two halves by two people, one of whom is lying on a trestle forty feet away.
setting.atmosphere: Work resumed. That is the strange thing about days three and four: the House goes back to its desks, because the Almanac has a printer's deadline and the printer does not care that the Master is dead. Pens and paper and the low argument about a decimal, exactly as before, with a sheet over a trestle in the undercroft. The party is now visibly investigating and the House is visibly aware of it, and the temperature of every conversation has dropped by about ten degrees without anybody being rude.

keyLocations.name: The Computing Rooms
keyLocations.description: Four long rooms of sloped desks, worked in pairs, each reckoner initialling the foot of every column they check. Shelves of three years of published Almanacs in bound quires and the House's own copies back to its founding.
features: Three years of published eastern frost tables, each quire signed off at the foot in a small upright hand: I.W.
The paired-checking system, designed so that no single person's error can reach print
Merrit Doane, who was helping Ardwen look and will show anyone the quires, loudly, with the wrong conclusion attached
encounters: Reading three years of tables, which takes a day unless somebody in the party can actually do the mathematics
The residents working around the party, politely, at a distance that gets larger each day
Ilsabet Wray, at her desk, offering to check the party's arithmetic
secrets: C5 lives here: the eastern frost dates for three years, each nine days late, each signed I.W.
The paired-checking system was not defeated. The eastern quires were signed by one person twice, which the House's own rules permit for a senior computer and which nobody has ever done before

keyLocations.name: The Master's Study
keyLocations.description: A small room at the end of the gallery passage with its own stove, its own lamp, and thirty-one years of day-books on a shelf. The current one is on the desk. A page has been cut out of it, close to the gutter, with a penknife that is lying open beside it.
features: Thirty-one years of day-books, one line for every day of a very ordered life
The current volume, with a page removed between the entries for the day before the death and the day of it
The errata sheet in draft, three attempts, all of them naming the House and none of them naming a person
A letter delivered that morning by the courier who turned straight round: the printer, confirming that the errata will be set and bound if the fair copy comes down with it
encounters: Reading a dead man's diary, which is unpleasant and productive
Halva Onn, who comes to the study twice and does not explain why, and who is looking for the vault sequence
The realisation that the errata sheet exists, is drafted, and is the motive for everything
secrets: The missing page is in the hall stove's ash-pan and has about a day left before the pan is emptied (C8)
The errata drafts name the House and not the signatory — Ardwen was going to publish the negligence and resign, and protect nobody, including himself

keyLocations.name: The Hall Stove
keyLocations.description: An iron stove at the side of the hall, banked at night and riddled each morning, whose ash-pan is emptied by the kitchen boy every fourth morning. On the third morning it contains a burned page that went in flat.
features: A banked fire that does not consume paper laid flat against cold ash
An ash-pan with about a day left before Jory Pike carries it out to the yard
Sennet Vole's chair, four feet away, where he sits at all hours because he sleeps badly
encounters: Searching an ash-pan in a room where people are eating breakfast
Sennet Vole, who heard someone at the stove in the small hours and can say roughly when
Jory Pike, who will empty the pan on the fourth morning unless somebody stops him, and who will not be told why
secrets: C8: the missing day-book page, burned but legible in patches — the other half of the confession
The page went into the stove at about three in the morning on the night of the death, and the person who put it there had cut it out with the dead man's own penknife

keyLocations.name: The Reckoning-Vault
keyLocations.description: An iron-bound door at the far end of the undercroft with a mechanism of six dials and two cranks set into its face, opening to a sequence held in two halves by the Master Reckoner and the Archivist. One half is now unavailable and the other is in Halva Onn's head and she will not turn it without the Master's seal.
features: Six dials, two cranks, and a mechanism that has been maintained for two hundred years and works perfectly
Two centuries of raw nightly observations racked inside, including the last three years of eastern frost readings
A brass plate on the door recording the founding rule: the vault opens to the Master and the Archivist together, and to no one else, ever
encounters: Halva Onn, who is an obstacle with a spine and not a villain, and who is right
The mechanism itself, which can be worked out from the House's own records by someone who understands the Almanac's mathematics
Ysobel Kirren, who could open it in an afternoon and will not, because it would show what else she has been doing with her tools
secrets: C6 is inside: the raw eastern observations for three years, every one of them correct, proving the error was made at publication and not at the instrument
Ardwen's half of the sequence is written in the day-books — not the missing page, but in the volume for the year he took office, where he recorded it as an ordinary line of a very ordered life

synopsis: The House goes back to work on the third morning, because the printer does not care that the Master is dead, and the party goes to work too. Upstairs there are three years of eastern frost tables each nine days late and each signed off in the same small upright hand, and a day-book with a page cut out of it, and three drafts of an errata sheet that would have bound the House's negligence into the spring Almanac. Downstairs there is a stove with an ash-pan that will be emptied tomorrow morning, and at the end of the undercroft an iron door that opens to a sequence one dead man and one living woman knew half of each. Behind that door are two centuries of raw observations, and they are the difference between a suspicion and a proof — and between a saved harvest and a lost one.
hook: You come down on the third morning expecting a House in mourning and find a House at work. Eight o'clock, desks manned, pens going, and the low argument about a decimal exactly as it was two days ago, because the fair copy goes down the pass at thaw and the printer has a press booked. Halva Onn is already in the passage outside the Master's study with a candle, trying the door. Merrit Doane is telling anyone who will hold still that Corwin Tace did it. Ilsabet Wray, at her desk, looks up as you come past and says — kindly, and meaning it — 'If you're going to read the tables, come to me. It's four hands and three years and half of it is in a shorthand nobody's written down. I'll show you the shorthand.'

acts.title: Act 1: Three Years of Nine Days
acts.description: The falsification, the signature on it, the missing page, and the motive — all of it available on the third day to a party willing to read. This act is quiet, textual, and where the campaign's second thread becomes visible.
objectives: Find the three years of falsified eastern frost tables and the signature at the foot (C5)
Search the Master's study and find the errata drafts and the cut page
Recover the burned page from the hall stove before the ash-pan is emptied (C8)
Understand that the harvest and the murder are two separate problems

scenes.name: The Quires
scenes.description: Three years of published tables, read properly. C5, and the point at which the campaign's second thread stops being background.
scenes.readAloud: "A bound quire of the Almanac is a beautiful object and an exhausting one: forty pages of six-column tables in four hands, every column initialled at the foot by two people, tide and frost and planting and market and eclipse, for every hundred in the province. You want six pages of it — the eastern frost dates, three years running — and finding them takes an hour. Reading them takes another, and understanding them takes somebody who can do a reduction. And when it comes, it comes all at once. Year before last, the eastern frost date is nine days late. Last year, nine days late. This year, nine days late. Three years, the same error, the same direction, the same size. And at the foot of all three, where two initials should be, there is one set, twice, in a small upright hand: I.W. — I.W."

skillChecks.success: C5. Three years of eastern frost dates, each nine days late, each signed off in the same hand, twice. The House's rules permit a senior computer to check their own work; nobody has ever done it before and there is no other instance of it in three years of quires.
skillChecks.failure: Columns of figures in four hands. You can see they are numbers and you cannot see which ones are wrong.

skillChecks.success: Same result as above by a different road: you know what the eastern hundreds' frost date is supposed to be for those years, roughly, from published record elsewhere, and these are nine days out.
skillChecks.failure: You are not a reckoner and this is a reckoner's document.

skillChecks.success: Ilsabet Wray offered to show you the shorthand, and she did, honestly and thoroughly, and she is still standing at your shoulder while you read her own signature at the foot of the eastern quires. She has not moved and she has not said anything. She is waiting to see whether you can read it.
skillChecks.failure: A helpful senior colleague, being helpful.

scenes.roleplayNotes: PLAY WRAY'S HELPFULNESS COMPLETELY STRAIGHT. She offers, she explains, she is good at it, and she does not steer the party away from anything — because steering them away would be a plan, and she has no plan. If a player asks her directly about the signature she says, truthfully and flatly, 'That's mine. I signed those.' And then she says: 'The Master found it a fortnight ago. I imagine that's what you're really asking.' She will not lie about the tables. She will only lie about where she was at a quarter past nine.
loot: C5: three years of eastern frost dates, nine days late, signed I.W. twice

scenes.name: The Study and the Cut Page
scenes.description: The Master's room: thirty-one years of day-books, three drafts of an errata sheet, a page cut out with a penknife, and the printer's letter that came up the pass the morning of the death.
scenes.readAloud: "Thirty-one years of day-books on a shelf, one line for every day, and the current volume open on the desk beside a penknife with the blade still out. Between the entry for the fourth of the month and the entry for the sixth, there is a stub about two fingers wide, cut close and cut carefully. And under the blotter, three attempts at the same document: 'ERRATA, to be bound into the Almanac of this year. The eastern frost tables for the three years preceding are in error by nine days. The error is the House's and was not detected by the House's own checking, and the Master Reckoner accepts —' and there it stops, and starts again, twice more, and in none of the three drafts is any individual named at all."

skillChecks.success: The page was cut with the knife on the desk, from this side, by somebody standing where you are standing. It was not torn out in a hurry; it was cut close to the gutter by someone taking their time in a room where they should not have been.
skillChecks.failure: A page missing from a diary. You do not know when it went.

skillChecks.success: Read the errata drafts again. He is not naming her. Three attempts and he never once writes the signature down — he takes it on the House and on himself and resigns. Whatever he told her in that study on the second night, this document was going to ruin him and shield her, and she almost certainly did not know that.
skillChecks.failure: A dry official document about an arithmetic error.

skillChecks.success: A letter, dated the day of the death, delivered by the courier who came up and turned round: the printer, confirming the press and asking whether the errata sheet is to be set. Ardwen received this at about noon and was dead by half past nine.
skillChecks.failure: The desk is tidy and there is a great deal of correspondence on it.

scenes.roleplayNotes: The errata drafts are the emotional key to the whole campaign and the players should meet them before they meet the culprit. Ardwen was going to publish, take the blame on the House and on himself, and name nobody. Ilsabet Wray killed him for a document that would not have carried her name. Do not point this out; let the players find it and let it sit.
loot: Three drafts of the errata sheet, naming the House and no individual
The printer's letter, dated the day of the death
The penknife, and a page-stub two fingers wide

scenes.name: The Ash-Pan
scenes.description: C8, on a clock. The page is in the hall stove, and Jory Pike empties the pan tomorrow morning. If the party is not in the hall today with their hands in the ash, it is gone.
scenes.readAloud: "The hall stove is a squat iron thing at the side of the room, banked overnight and riddled each morning, with an ash-pan underneath that pulls out on a handle. There are people at breakfast eleven feet away. There is an old man asleep in a chair four feet away. Kneeling down in front of it and pulling the pan out is a socially ridiculous thing to do and you should feel that as you do it. Inside there is grey ash, and clinker, and — lying flat against the cold back of the pan where the fire never reached — most of a page of paper, brown and brittle and burned to lace at the edges, with handwriting still on it."

skillChecks.success: C8. You get the page out in three pieces and enough of it survives to read: '...spoke to I.W. She asks for time. There is no time; the copy goes down at thaw and I will not send it down false... errata bound in, and my own name to the negligence of the House...' It is Ardwen's hand and it is the entry for the day he died.
skillChecks.failure: Ash, clinker and the corner of something that might have been paper, which crumbles between your fingers. ALTERNATE ROUTE: Sennet Vole heard someone at the stove in the small hours and can say roughly when — that gets the party back to the pan for one more attempt at advantage, and it costs a day. IF THE PAN IS EMPTIED FIRST, THE PAGE IS GONE and the case must be closed on C3 and the timeline instead.

skillChecks.success: Sennet Vole is four feet away with his eyes shut and he says, without preamble, 'Somebody was at that stove at about three. I heard the pan.' Nobody has asked him anything in four years and he is delighted.
skillChecks.failure: An old man asleep by a fire while you kneel in the ashes.

scenes.roleplayNotes: C8 IS ON A CLOCK AND THE DM MUST RUN THE CLOCK. Jory Pike empties the ash-pan on the fourth morning, as he does every fourth morning, and he will do it while the party is at breakfast unless somebody has thought to stop him. Say it plainly when it happens: 'The boy carries the pan out to the yard and tips it.' If the page is lost, the campaign still works — Wray can be brought to confession on C3 plus the timeline plus Vole's testimony, though it is harder and takes the whole of rh-scenario-004. Do not restore a lost C8 under any circumstances.
loot: C8: the burned day-book page — the other half of the confession

acts.title: Act 2: The Weight on the Wrong Hook
acts.description: The orrery, the coat in the drying loft, and Ysobel Kirren — who can read the campaign's most elegant clue in a second and who is hiding something entirely unrelated. This act narrows the field from twelve to three.
objectives: Examine the orrery and find the sun-weight on the wrong hook (C2)
Search the drying loft, or be kind to Nan Gaddy, and find the coat (C4)
Establish which three residents wear House-coats of that cut
Deal with Ysobel Kirren's entirely separate guilt without wasting three days on it

scenes.name: The Hooks Along the Plinth
scenes.description: C2. A four-pound brass weight hanging two hooks from where it belongs, in plain sight of everyone, in the middle of the hall.
scenes.readAloud: "The orrery is the most beautiful object in the building and everybody in the House has stopped seeing it. Brass sun, brass moon, six planets on jointed arms, a hand-crank at the base, and along the rim of the plinth a row of small hooks with the counterweights hanging from them, each hook with a brass plate under it in engraved capitals: SOL. LUNA. And then the six. The weights are pear-shaped, four pounds or so, on bronze eyes, polished to the same soft gold as everything else on this plinth. Except one. On the hook labelled MARS there is a weight, and it is brighter than its neighbours — recently and thoroughly cleaned — and the hook labelled SOL, two along, is empty."

skillChecks.success: C2. The sun-weight is on the wrong hook and its polish is fresher than every other weight on the plinth, and there is a fine dark line in the seam where the eye meets the body of it that a cloth would not reach.
skillChecks.failure: Brass, gears, and a great many small hooks with small labels. It is beautiful and it tells you nothing. ALTERNATE ROUTE: ask Ysobel Kirren whether anything about the orrery is wrong. She will see it in a second.

skillChecks.success: Whoever put it back knew the orrery well enough to rehang it at all — a stranger would simply have dropped it or taken it away. And they were rattled enough to get the hook wrong by two, in a room they use every day. That narrows this House considerably.
skillChecks.failure: A weight on a hook.

skillChecks.success: The curved margin of the fracture on the body in the cold-store matches the shoulder of this weight. It is not a conclusive match by any standard you would care to defend, and it is close enough to be certain in your own mind.
skillChecks.failure: A brass weight and a broken head. You cannot make the comparison from memory.

scenes.roleplayNotes: C2's alternate route is Ysobel Kirren, and it costs a conversation rather than a day — but the conversation opens her own guilt, which is about brass fittings and not about murder, and she will assume she is being accused of the killing and behave exactly like someone who is guilty of something. That is the trap in this clue and it is a fair one.
loot: C2: the sun-weight on the hook marked MARS, freshly polished, with a dark line in the seam

scenes.name: Ysobel Kirren's Afternoon
scenes.description: The instrument-wright, who knows every hook by name and has no alibi and has been quietly melting down the orrery's spare fittings. A whole scene of a person being guilty of the wrong thing.
scenes.readAloud: "She is in her workshop off the undercroft and she does not look up when you come in, which is a decision rather than a habit. There is a small furnace, a bench, a rack of files, and a set of scales. When you ask her about the plinth she answers before you have finished the question: 'MARS. It's on MARS. I saw it on the morning after and I have not been able to look at it since and I have not said anything to anybody, because I have no more idea than you do where I was at nine o'clock that anyone can swear to, and I have —' and she stops, and her hands go still on the bench, and she says, in a completely different voice, 'and I have been doing something else, and I would rather be hanged for the wrong thing than explain the right one.'"

skillChecks.success: She tells you the whole of it in ninety seconds and it is nothing: she has been melting the orrery's spare brass fittings and casting them into small stock to sell at thaw, because she is paid four pounds a year and has a sister in the village. She is stealing from a machine she loves and she is ashamed of it in a way that is out of all proportion.
skillChecks.failure: She will not say and she will not be pushed, and she becomes the party's second-best suspect for two days, entirely on the strength of being frightened.

skillChecks.success: Whatever she is hiding, she is not hiding a murder. She is hiding something that would end her employment, and the difference in how a person holds those two secrets is visible if you have ever seen both.
skillChecks.failure: She is terrified and evasive and has no alibi and knows the murder weapon by name. If you were making a list, she would be on it.

scenes.roleplayNotes: Kirren is not one of the three official herrings and should not be run as one — she is the campaign's demonstration that in a closed House everybody has a secret and most of the secrets are small. Let the party spend an hour on her, not a day. If they are kind, she gives them C2 outright and becomes their best source on the orrery for the rest of the campaign.

scenes.name: The Drying Loft
scenes.description: C4. Twelve House-coats over the kitchen flue, one of them laundered with lamp-oil and brass polish still in the cuff — and Nan Gaddy, who will simply tell the party if they have earned it.
scenes.readAloud: "The drying loft is directly under the roof, where the kitchen flue runs up through it, and it is the only genuinely warm place in the building and smells overwhelmingly of wet wool. Everything the House owns that has been washed this week is up here on lines: shirts, linen, and a dozen House-coats of the same heavy grey cut, hanging shoulder to shoulder like a committee. Nan Gaddy is up here with a basket, and she is talking before you have got up the last three steps, because Nan Gaddy talks to anyone who is not grand and there is nobody up here to interrupt her."

skillChecks.success: C4. One coat has been washed and still carries lamp-oil in the weave at the right cuff, and worked into it, grey-black and unmistakable once you have your nose in it, brass polish. It is a size and cut worn by three residents.
skillChecks.failure: Twelve identical grey coats, all of them smelling of lamp-oil, because every room in this House is lit by lamps.

skillChecks.success: ALTERNATE ROUTE, and it is deliberately easy: be a person rather than an investigator for four minutes and Nan Gaddy volunteers it. 'A coat came to me on the third morning with polish on the cuff, and I thought that was odd, because who polishes anything in winter? Nobody's touched that orrery since Ysobel did it on the Tuesday.'
skillChecks.failure: She talks for twenty minutes about the flue, the damp, her sister's husband, and the price of soda, and none of it is what you came for, and it is your own fault.

skillChecks.success: She does not know whose coat it was and is not being coy. She washes for twelve people and coats come to her in a basket.
skillChecks.failure: You suspect the laundress of withholding, which she is not, and she notices, and that door closes.

scenes.roleplayNotes: C4 narrows the field to three — Wray, Onn and Kirren — and it must not narrow it to one. If a player tries to identify the specific coat by size or wear, the honest answer is that the three are within an inch of each other and the House-coats are pooled and shared at the wash. This clue is a filter, not an accusation, and the DM should hold that line.
loot: C4: a House-coat, laundered, with lamp-oil and brass polish in the right cuff — narrowing the field to Wray, Onn and Kirren

acts.title: Act 3: The Mechanism
acts.description: The vault. Six dials, two cranks, a sequence held in two halves, an archivist who will not turn her half without a seal that no longer exists, and two hundred years of raw observations that are the difference between suspicion and proof. The climax of the scenario and the only place in the campaign where C6 can be had.
objectives: Persuade or outmanoeuvre Halva Onn without making an enemy of her
Recover Ardwen's half of the sequence from the day-books
Find the raw eastern observations and prove the error was made at publication (C6)

scenes.name: Halva Onn Says No
scenes.description: An obstacle with a spine and not a villain. She is right, she knows she is right, and she will not be moved by any argument that is actually available to the party.
scenes.readAloud: "She meets you at the vault door, which suggests she has been expecting this conversation and has decided where to have it. Behind her, set into two inches of oak and iron, are six brass dials and two cranks, and above them a plate that has been there for two hundred years: THIS VAULT OPENS TO THE MASTER AND THE ARCHIVIST TOGETHER AND TO NO OTHER, EVER. She lets you read it. Then she says: 'I have my half. I have had it for eleven years and I will have it until I die or I am replaced. The Master had the other and the Master is on a trestle forty feet behind you. So: no. Not because I doubt you, and not because I have anything in there I mind you seeing. Because the rule is the rule and it is two hundred years old and it has held through two fires and a plague, and I am not going to be the archivist who broke it in a week because some couriers had a theory.'"

skillChecks.success: There is exactly one argument that works and it is not about the murder: the eastern hundreds will plant nine days early on a printed frost date unless the raw observations prove the error, and Halva Onn has a brother farming in the eastern hundreds. She turns her half. She does it with her eyes shut and she does not speak for the rest of the day.
skillChecks.failure: 'No.' She is not angry and she does not become an enemy. She simply does not move, and she will not move for this argument again.

skillChecks.success: She is not protecting a secret. She is protecting a rule, and the rule is the only thing in this building she has ever been given sole charge of. Attacking her integrity will fail completely; giving her a reason that outranks the rule is the only road.
skillChecks.failure: An obstructive archivist. Some people simply like saying no.

skillChecks.success: You get nothing at all and you should not get anything. A party that threatens Halva Onn has lost the vault for the rest of the campaign and should be told so plainly through her behaviour rather than by the DM.
skillChecks.failure: She looks at you for a long moment and then walks away and does not speak to any of you again before thaw.

scenes.roleplayNotes: NEVER PLAY HALVA ONN AS A VILLAIN OR AS A PUZZLE TO BE BEATEN. She is correct. The party's route through her is to find something that outranks the rule — the harvest, and her brother in the eastern hundreds — and if they have not learned about her brother yet, that is what Oriel Fenn and Nan Gaddy are for. If they get the sequence another way and open the vault without her, she finds out within a day and the House turns markedly colder for the rest of the campaign, which is a fair price and should be paid.

scenes.name: One Line in a Very Ordered Life
scenes.description: Ardwen's half of the sequence, recorded in the day-book for the year he took office as an ordinary entry, because he wrote a line about every day of his life for thirty-one years and saw no reason to make an exception.
scenes.readAloud: "Thirty-one volumes. One line a day. Weather, work, health, and the occasional flat observation about a colleague that reads like a knife when you come across it. The volume for the year he took office is the eleventh from the left, and the entry for the day he was sworn is four lines long, which for Hollis Ardwen is practically a psalm — and the fourth line reads: 'Given the Master's half. SOL 4, LUNA 1, then the six as they stand at midwinter. I record it here because I shall forget it otherwise and there is nobody living I would rather trust with it than this book.'"

skillChecks.success: You find it in about two hours of reading, which is fast. The sequence is there and it is written down in the plainest possible language by a man who did not believe in secrets, only in records.
skillChecks.failure: Thirty-one years of one-line entries and you are somewhere in the seventh volume when your candle goes. Try again tomorrow: this clue does not expire, it only costs time.

skillChecks.success: 'The six as they stand at midwinter' is an astronomical instruction, not a code: set the six planet-dials to the positions the orrery itself shows for midwinter. The machine in the hall is the key to the door in the cellar, which is either very elegant or very smug depending on how you feel about the founders.
skillChecks.failure: The first two dials are numbers and the rest is a sentence about planets. You need someone who can read the sky.

skillChecks.success: Same result by another road: any character who has spent time at the orrery, or asks Ysobel Kirren, can produce the midwinter positions in five minutes.
skillChecks.failure: Astronomy is not your field.

scenes.roleplayNotes: This is the campaign's one piece of puzzle-solving and it is deliberately fair: the answer is written down in plain language and the only obstacle is the labour of reading thirty-one volumes. Emmerich Vause the wizard is built for this and should get the moment. If the party has already got Onn's cooperation, this scene is a pleasure rather than a necessity; if they have not, it is the only road.
loot: Ardwen's half of the vault sequence: SOL 4, LUNA 1, and the six as they stand at midwinter

scenes.name: Two Hundred Years of Nights
scenes.description: The vault opens. C6, and the campaign's second thread becomes solvable.
scenes.readAloud: "The mechanism does not stick and does not groan; it has been oiled every quarter for two hundred years and it turns like something that was made properly. The door comes back on its pin and the air that comes out is cold and dry and smells of paper and nothing else. It is not a treasury. It is a room of racked observation books, floor to ceiling, two centuries deep: every night that anyone at this House has looked at the sky and written down what was there, in the hands of forty dead reckoners, bound in fifties, dated on the spine. The last three years are on the near rack at shoulder height because they are the ones people actually use. And the eastern frost readings for all three years, taken at the instrument, night after night, are correct. Every one of them. Every single one."

skillChecks.success: C6. The raw observations are correct and the published tables are nine days out, which means the error entered between the instrument and the press. It was made at publication, by a person, at a desk, and it was signed for.
skillChecks.failure: Two centuries of racked observation books and a great deal of very small handwriting. Come back tomorrow with a lamp and someone who can read a reduction; the vault is open now and stays open.

skillChecks.success: With C5 and C6 together you can write the correction yourself, and it will hold up in front of the printer. The harvest is now saveable — provided somebody can get a correction into the fair copy before it is sealed, which is an entirely separate and much more social problem.
skillChecks.failure: You have the proof and you cannot yet do anything with it.

scenes.roleplayNotes: C6 HAS NO ALTERNATE ROUTE, which is why the vault is a scenario and not a lock. If the party never opens it, the harvest thread can still be won in rh-scenario-004 by persuading the House on the strength of C5 alone — harder, and dependent on the room, and genuinely uncertain. End the scenario here, with the vault open and the party in possession of a proof about the harvest and a suspicion about the murder, and the two of them not yet connected.
loot: C6: three years of raw eastern frost observations, all correct — the error was made at publication
Access to the vault for the remainder of the campaign

npcsInvolved.name: Ilsabet Wray, 54
npcsInvolved.description: In this scenario she is helpful, competent and entirely present. She offers to teach the party the House's shorthand and does so thoroughly. She does not lie about the tables and will confirm her own signature flatly if asked. She lies about exactly one thing: where she was at a quarter past nine on the second night.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Not money. She signed off three years of eastern frost tables without checking the reduction, out of overwork and pride, and Ardwen's errata sheet would have bound the House's negligence and her signature into an Almanac that every farm keeps on a nail for a year. She went up to ask him to hold it one season; he refused; she picked up the weight. She had no plan and has no second one. She has no plan and no second one. Under suspicion she gets quieter, not louder, and she is visibly relieved when the House turns on Tace, and hates herself for it.

npcsInvolved.name: Halva Onn, 40
npcsInvolved.description: Holds half a two-hundred-year-old sequence and will not turn it without the Master's seal, which no longer exists. Not obstructive, not hiding anything, and completely immovable by any argument about the murder. She has a brother farming in the eastern hundreds and that is the only lever in the building.
npcsInvolved.motivation: The rule is the rule. It has held through two fires and a plague and she is not going to be the archivist who broke it in a week.

npcsInvolved.name: Ysobel Kirren, 34
npcsInvolved.description: Saw the sun-weight on the wrong hook the morning after and has said nothing to anybody, because she has no alibi and because she has been melting the orrery's spare fittings and casting them into stock to sell at thaw. She is guilty of the wrong thing and will behave exactly like someone guilty of the right one.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Four pounds a year, a sister in the village, and a machine she loves and is stealing from.

npcsInvolved.name: Nan Gaddy, 38
npcsInvolved.description: Talks to anyone kind and to nobody grand. Found a coat with polish in the cuff on the third morning and thought it odd because nobody polishes anything in winter. Will hand this over for the price of four minutes of ordinary human conversation and nothing at all for the price of an interrogation.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Company, and being treated as a person by somebody in this building.

npcsInvolved.name: Sennet Vole, 70
npcsInvolved.role: Emeritus / Heard the stove at three
npcsInvolved.description: Sits by the hall fire at all hours because he sleeps badly, and heard the ash-pan pulled out at about three on the night of the death. He can time anything by the chimes and nobody has asked him a question in four years. He is the alternate route to C8 and he is delighted to be consulted.

npcsInvolved.name: Merrit Doane, 22
npcsInvolved.description: Will show the party the eastern quires immediately and loudly, with the conclusion 'and that is why Tace killed him' attached to it. He helped Ardwen find the falsification and does not understand what it means. If allowed into the investigation he will tell the whole House everything the party finds within the hour.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To have been important to a dead man. He is entirely innocent and entirely destructive.

npcsInvolved.name: Corwin Tace, 47
npcsInvolved.description: By day four the House has largely decided he did it, on Merrit Doane's evidence, which is no evidence. He responds by becoming harder to find and lying about everything, which confirms it for everybody. His alibi is airtight and comes from Oriel Fenn, and he will not claim it himself because at nine o'clock he was falsifying an entry in the tally book.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To keep the strongbox shut. He would rather be suspected of murder for a week than have three letters read aloud.

rewards.gold: None. This campaign has no treasure and the DM should stop looking for a way to insert some. The vault contains paper.
items: C5 — three years of eastern frost tables, each nine days late, each signed I.W. twice
C8 — the burned day-book page from the hall stove, if recovered before the pan was emptied
C2 — the sun-weight on the hook marked MARS, freshly polished, with a dark line in the seam
C4 — a laundered House-coat with lamp-oil and brass polish in the right cuff, narrowing the field to three
C6 — two hundred years of raw observations, and three years of correct eastern frost readings
Three drafts of Ardwen's errata sheet, naming the House and no individual
The printer's letter, dated the day of the death
Ardwen's half of the vault sequence, and standing access to the vault
rewards.story: The party can now prove that the eastern frost tables were falsified at publication and not at the instrument, and they can name the signature at the foot of them. They have a weight on the wrong hook, a coat that narrows the House to three, and — if they were fast enough with the ash-pan — a dead man's own account of the conversation that killed him. What they do not have is a person at the top of that stair at a quarter past nine. Four days left, an archivist who may not be speaking to them, and a bursar the entire House has decided is guilty.

twists: The errata sheet names nobody. Three drafts, and in none of them does Ardwen write Ilsabet Wray's name — he takes it on the House and on himself and resigns. She killed him for a document that would have protected her, and she did not know.

Ilsabet Wray does not lie about the tables. She confirms her own signature flatly the moment she is asked, and offers to teach the party the shorthand they need to read her own falsification. She lies about exactly one thing all campaign: where she was at a quarter past nine.

The vault's sequence was written down in plain language by a man who did not believe in secrets, in a day-book, thirty-one volumes ago — and half of it is an instruction to read the orrery in the hall. The machine everybody has stopped seeing is the key to the door in the cellar.

Ysobel Kirren saw the weight on the wrong hook on the first morning and said nothing for four days, not to protect anyone, but because she is stealing brass from the orrery and would rather be suspected of murder than have that come out. In a closed House everybody has a secret and almost all of them are small.
The clock is a boy with an ash-pan. C8 disappears on the fourth morning because Jory Pike carries the ashes out to the yard as he does every fourth morning, and nobody has told him not to.
dmTips: RUN THE ASH-PAN CLOCK HONESTLY. Jory Pike empties the stove on the fourth morning. If the party has not searched it or stopped him, describe him carrying the pan out and tipping it, in plain language, at breakfast, and do not restore the page afterwards under any circumstances. If C8 is lost the campaign still finishes — Wray can be brought to a confession on C3 plus the timeline plus Sennet Vole — but it takes the whole of rh-scenario-004 and it is genuinely harder, which is the correct consequence.

PLAY ILSABET WRAY AS THE MOST HELPFUL PERSON IN THE BUILDING and do not tip her once. She teaches the party the shorthand, she confirms her own signature without hesitation, she fetches a blanket for whoever is cold. Every instinct you have to make her furtive is wrong: she has no plan, and a person with no plan behaves normally right up until they cannot.

HALVA ONN IS RIGHT AND MUST NOT BE PLAYED AS A VILLAIN. The vault rule is two hundred years old and has survived two fires and a plague. The only argument that moves her is the harvest and her brother in the eastern hundreds, and if the party has not learned about the brother, that is what Oriel Fenn and Nan Gaddy exist for. Threatening her costs the party the vault permanently and the DM should let that stand.

OFFER THE ALTERNATE ROUTES IN FICTION, NOT AS A DM ANNOUNCEMENT. If the party misses C2, have Ysobel Kirren be visibly unable to look at the plinth. If they miss C4, have Nan Gaddy start talking to whoever is kindest. If they miss C8's first attempt, have Sennet Vole say 'somebody was at that stove at about three' without being asked. Each alternate route costs a day; say so by having the day pass, not by narrating the cost.

NEVER STATE THE SOLUTION. If a player asks you out of character who did it, decline warmly and give them a lead. If a player asks an NPC directly, the NPC does not know. The only person in this building who knows is Ilsabet Wray and she will not say until C3 and C8 are put in front of her together.

DO NOT MERGE THE TWO THREADS. C5 and C6 solve the harvest and say nothing about the murder except that a motive exists. C1, C2, C3, C4, C8 and C9 solve the murder and do nothing for the harvest. The party can win either, both or neither, and the DM must resist every instinct to make one resolve the other.

LET THE HOUSE CONVICT TACE. By the end of this scenario the residents have largely decided the bursar did it, on Merrit Doane's say-so, which is not evidence. Play the social temperature accordingly: people who were friendly on day two are curt on day four, and Tace himself becomes almost impossible to find. This is herring H1 doing exactly what it is for, and the disproof (Oriel Fenn, and the tally book taking an hour to write up) is available whenever the party thinks to ask her properly.

THIS SCENARIO HAS NO COMBAT AND SHOULD NOT ACQUIRE ANY. Three set-pieces exist in the whole campaign and both of the remaining two are in scenarios three and four. If the table is restless, give them the vault mechanism and the thirty-one day-books; that is the puzzle-focus dial this campaign was built around.

EMMERICH VAUSE IS BUILT FOR THIS SCENARIO. The wizard is the only outsider who can read the Almanac's mathematics, and C5, C6 and the midwinter dials are all his. If a player is running him, hand him all three. If not, run him as a companion and let him do the arithmetic and be wrong about the people.
PACE IT AS TWO SESSIONS: the quires, the study and the ash-pan; then the orrery, the coat, Kirren, and the vault. End on the vault open and the two threads still not touching.
